questions.q: What does a real provider console's device map typically show, beyond the chip's basic connectivity graph?
options: A single overall score for the entire chip with no per-qubit detail
Only an abstract diagram with no connection to any real measured performance
The chip's manufacturing date and nothing else
Live or recent calibration data overlaid on the nodes and edges, such as per-qubit error/coherence numbers and per-edge two-qubit gate error rates
questions.explain: A device map combines the static connectivity graph with real, usually regularly updated calibration data -- per-qubit error and coherence numbers, and per-edge two-qubit gate error rates -- not just a static wiring diagram.

questions.q: Why can two edges that look identical in a chip's topology diagram have measurably different real two-qubit error rates?
options: Error rates are randomly reassigned by the software each time the map is viewed
Edges only differ in error rate if they connect qubits on opposite sides of the chip
Topologically identical edges always have mathematically identical error rates on real hardware
Qubit-to-qubit manufacturing variation and local calibration drift mean nominally similar connections can perform differently in practice
questions.explain: Real chips show qubit-to-qubit manufacturing variation and drift over time, so two edges that look the same in the topology diagram can show meaningfully different measured error rates -- sometimes by a factor of two or more.

questions.q: What is a chip's 'sweet spot,' in the context of reading a device map?
options: Any region of the chip, since all regions perform identically
A cluster of adjacent qubits and edges currently showing comparatively low error rates, worth prioritizing for a circuit's most error-sensitive gates
The region of the chip physically closest to the dilution refrigerator's coldest point
The single qubit that was fabricated most recently
questions.explain: A sweet spot is a region of currently low-error, well-performing qubits and edges on the same chip -- identifying it is exactly what practitioners look for when reading a live device map, rather than just asking 'is this chip good.'

questions.q: Why is choosing which physical qubits to map a circuit onto considered a real optimization step rather than a formality?
options: Every physical qubit on a chip always performs identically, so selection doesn't matter
Qubit selection has no measurable effect on a circuit's outcome, so it's purely procedural

Mapping a circuit's most error-sensitive gates onto currently well-performing physical qubits, instead of a naive default assignment, can meaningfully change the real-world result without changing any logical gate
Qubit selection is handled entirely by the hardware with no input possible from the circuit designer
questions.explain: Because real error rates vary across a chip, deliberately choosing well-performing physical qubits for error-sensitive gates is a genuine lever with a measurable payoff -- not a courtesy step before the 'real' work.

questions.q: When a chip's lowest-error region (a 'sweet spot') doesn't match a circuit's required connectivity pattern, what tension does the lesson say a practitioner actually has to weigh?
options: Error quality versus connectivity fit -- a low-error region that needs added SWAPs to fit the circuit may be worse overall than a slightly higher-error region that already matches the circuit's connectivity natively
The only consideration is total qubit count, never error rate or connectivity
Connectivity fit is irrelevant as long as the chip map shows any edges at all
There is no real tension, since the lowest-error region is always the correct choice regardless of connectivity
questions.explain: A region with excellent error rates but poor connectivity fit may need extra SWAPs (with their own added error), potentially making it a worse real choice than a region with middling error rates but native connectivity -- a genuine tradeoff only the live device map can inform.
